Partitions for moving norms and smooth separation

Written by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), October 2026. Public domain (CC0).

A local measuring ball may change its size and shape from point to point. Slow variation is enough to build a smooth partition whose derivatives obey one prescribed sequence of bounds, even when the norms themselves are discontinuous. We separate the geometric counting argument from the derivative calculation. The construction also gives a smooth function separating two closed sets away from their intersection.

The summable cutoff theorem, Theorem 3, supplies compact cutoffs in any fixed finite-dimensional norm with constant . The scalar foundation, Sections 12.5–12.9, proves compactness, countable coordinate bases and norm comparisons. The integration foundation proves the volume scaling used in packing. We use the same explicit set-theoretic maximality axiom as the functional foundation, Section 19. All applications of that axiom, all covering bounds, and all partition derivatives are proved here.

Let be a real vector space of dimension , let be open, and let be a norm on for each . The vector argument of a norm always belongs to ; the subscript is its measuring point. Write

Each of these is an open ball for a fixed norm. No differentiability, or even continuity, of is assumed.

Proof of selection and countability. Order all subsets of satisfying (M7) by inclusion. The empty set belongs. The union of a chain satisfies (M7), since any two of its points occur together in one member of the chain. The maximality axiom gives a maximal set. For each selected point , its ball contains no other selected point. Choose the first member of a fixed countable rational-coordinate basis which contains and is contained in this ball. Different selected points receive different basis members: a common member would contain both of them and violate (M7). This injects the set of centers into a countable set, giving the asserted enumeration. A finite family is allowed.

Lemma 3 (product estimate). At a fixed point , suppose smooth scalar functions obey and for a fixed norm and constants . Their product obeys the same estimate with .

Proof. Repeated directional differentiation assigns each of the labeled directions to one factor. If factor receives directions, its denominator is . Concatenate the lists for the separate factors. The index in each list is no larger than its position in the concatenation, so monotonicity gives The absolute value of that product-rule term is therefore at most . Summing over all assignments gives , by the finite distributive law. Factors receiving no derivative contribute at most one. The zeroth-order product is also at most one. This proves the statement, including zero constants.
